en.title: Glacier National Park
en.summary: Glacier National Park is a United States national park in the Rocky Mountains of northwestern Montana, established in 1910 as the nation's tenth national park. Known for the glacier-carved scenery of its Belt Supergroup sedimentary rocks, it has watched its namesake alpine glaciers shrink under a warming climate. Together with Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park it forms an International Peace Park and World Heritage Site.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Overview and location

Glacier National Park is a United States national park in the Rocky Mountains of northwestern Montana, adjoining the Canadian border. It was established as a park on May 11, 1910. [1] Two mountain ranges, the Livingston Range and the more easterly Lewis Range, run from northwest to southeast through the park, and the Continental Divide of the Americas follows the crest of the Lewis Range. [2]

The park covers 1,012,837 acres (1,583 square miles) with 205 miles of exterior boundary, of which 21 miles are shared with Waterton Lakes National Park and 31 miles with British Columbia. [1] Elevations run from a low of 3,150 feet (960 m) near the junction of the Middle and North Forks of the Flathead River, across 175 mountains, with Logan Pass at 6,646 feet (2,025 m). The highest summit is Mount Cleveland, though the park's own pages differ: the fact sheet gives 10,448 feet (3,190 m), while the geology page gives 10,466 feet (3,192 m). [1]

Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park was established in 1932, the same year the Going-to-the-Sun Road was completed. The park became an International Biosphere Reserve in 1974 and the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park World Heritage Site in 1995. [1]

## Four stages of geology

The park's mountains and valleys were formed over about 1.4 billion years by geologic processes including erosion, sediment deposition, uplift, faulting, and glaciation. The Park Service summarizes the story as "silt, tilt, slide, and glide." [2]

In the first stage, sand and silt were deposited into the Belt Sea, an inland sea of the middle Proterozoic Era about 1,500 million years ago that covered parts of present-day eastern Washington, northern Idaho, western Montana, and nearby Canada. Over roughly 100 million years the sediment reached a thickness of 18,000 feet (5,500 meters). [2] Heat and pressure compressed the [sediment](/hubpedia/sediment) into layers of quartzite, argillite, mudstone, limestone, and dolomite — the Belt Supergroup — visible above treeline in much of the park, where preserved mud cracks, ripples, and layering testify to the ancient sea. [2]

The rocks' colors are explained by iron chemistry. Iron in the argillite oxidized to red and purple when the retreating Belt Sea exposed it to air, while on the oxygen-free seafloor reduction bonded iron to silica compounds, and heat and pressure converted the iron-silicate minerals to chlorite, producing the green and blue rocks. [2] About 780 million years ago magma forced itself between layers of Siyeh Limestone, forming the Purcell Sill, a dark band of diorite about 100 feet (30 m) thick whose heat recrystallized the surrounding limestone into white marble. There is no naturally occurring granite in the park. [2]

When [tectonic plates](/hubpedia/plate-tectonics) collided at what was then the western edge of North America about 150 million years ago, massive forces pushed a stack of 1.5-to-1.4-billion-year-old sedimentary rock up and over much younger, only 70-million-year-old rocks along the Lewis Overthrust. The stack slid 50 miles (80 km) eastward over millions of years, at millimeters per year, one [earthquake](/hubpedia/earthquake) at a time. [2] In the Pleistocene ice age beginning about two million years ago, large ice sheets repeatedly advanced and retreated across temperate North America until ice left the area about 10,000 years ago. Massive U-shaped valleys, cirque lakes or tarns, horns, moraines, and arêtes are the glacially carved landforms that shape today's scenery. [2]

## The glaciers today and their retreat

A [glacier](/hubpedia/glacier) is a mass of ice so big it flows under its own weight. The commonly used size threshold is an area of 0.1 km², about 25 acres; below it the ice is less likely to move and is not considered a glacier. [3]

Around 1850, at the end of the Little Ice Age, about 80 glaciers occupied what would become the park. About 80 remained at the park's establishment in 1910; today there are roughly two dozen. [3] Aerial imagery from 2015 counted 26 named glaciers meeting the 0.1 km² criterion, nine fewer than in 1966. The park also hosts several unnamed glaciers, about a dozen rock glaciers, and many snowfields; a 2016 master's thesis using satellite imagery counted 13 rock glaciers and 14 formations that used to be rock glaciers. [3]

Between 1966 and 2015 every named glacier got smaller, some by more than 80 percent. The fact sheet records all 26 glaciers as shrinking and names Harrison Glacier as the largest. [3] Today's alpine glaciers are relatively recent, probably formed within the last 6,000 to 8,000 years, and likely grew rapidly during the Little Ice Age, which began 400 to 500 years ago and ended about 1850. Tree-ring studies indicate retreat began around 1850, stayed slow until about 1910, then accelerated in the mid- to late 1920s amid warmer summers and decreased precipitation; several larger glaciers split in two, such as the Jackson and Blackfoot Glaciers and the Grinnell and Salamander Glaciers. [2]

Glaciers shrink when summer melting outpaces winter snowfall. The decline since the end of the Little Ice Age is due to both natural and human-caused climate change, though retreat in recent decades is increasingly attributed to anthropogenic causes. [3] In 2003 researchers published a model predicting advance or retreat of Blackfoot Glacier and Jackson Glacier for each decade from 1990 to 2100; an informal estimate that they could be gone by 2030, later moved up to 2020, spread to park exhibits, which were updated in 2019 as the science advanced — the timing is now described as uncertain. [3]

Glacier meltwater supports irrigation for agriculture, cold streams for wildlife, and lakes for recreation. The national park itself was named for its many active glaciers. [3] North Cascades National Park holds the highest concentration of glaciers in the lower 48 states, while Glacier comes second with about two dozen active glaciers. [3]

## Lakes, streams, and wildlife

The park holds 762 lakes — 131 named and 631 unnamed. The largest, Lake McDonald, runs 9.4 miles long and 1.5 miles wide, is 464 feet deep, and covers 6,823 acres. [1] There are 563 streams totaling 2,865 miles (4,610 km) inside the park, the longest being Upper McDonald Creek at 25.8 miles (41.5 km). [1]

Recorded species include 71 mammals, 276 birds, 24 fish (18 native and 7 non-native), and 1,132 vascular plus 858 non-vascular plants. [1] The trail system counts 158 trails over 745.9 miles, including 110 miles of the Continental Divide Trail. [1] Visitation grew from 4,000 in 1911 to 3,049,839 in 2019. [1]

## Human history and the park's creation

Human use of the area dates back more than 10,000 years. When the first European explorers arrived, the Blackfeet Indians controlled the vast prairies east of the mountains while the Salish and Kootenai lived in the western valleys, crossing the mountains to hunt the great buffalo herds of the eastern plains. [4] The Kootenai referred to the area as Ya·qawiswit̓xuki, meaning "the place where there is a lot of ice." [3]

Most early European explorers came for beaver and other pelts, followed by miners and settlers looking for land. The completion of the Great Northern Railway in 1891 brought people into the heart of northwest Montana, and homesteaders settled the valleys west of Marias Pass, where small towns soon developed. [4] By the late 1800s, influential leaders like George Bird Grinnell pushed for a national park, and in 1910 President Taft signed the bill establishing Glacier as the country's 10th national park. [4]

## 出典

1. [Fact Sheet — Glacier National Park](https://www.nps.gov/glac/learn/news/fact-sheet.htm)
2. [Geologic Formations — Glacier National Park](https://www.nps.gov/glac/learn/nature/geologicformations.htm)
3. [Glacier's Glaciers — Glacier National Park](https://www.nps.gov/glac/learn/nature/glaciersoverview.htm)
4. [History & Culture — Glacier National Park](https://www.nps.gov/glac/learn/historyculture/index.htm)

articles.canonicalName: グレートスモーキー山脈国立公園
articles.description: グレートスモーキー山脈国立公園は、ノースカロライナ州とテネシー州の州境にまたがるアメリカ合衆国の国立公園で、全米で最も訪問者が多く、最も生物多様性の高い国立公園でもある。南アパラチアの古い山々に広がり、世界遺産および国際生物圏保護区に指定されている。
articles.title: グレートスモーキー山脈国立公園
articles.summary: グレートスモーキー山脈国立公園は、ノースカロライナ州とテネシー州の州境にまたがるアメリカ合衆国の国立公園で、全米で最も訪問者が多く、最も生物多様性の高い国立公園でもある。南アパラチアの古い山々に広がり、世界遺産および国際生物圏保護区に指定されている。
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 概要と地勢

グレートスモーキー山脈国立公園は、ノースカロライナ州とテネシー州の州境にまたがるアメリカ合衆国の国立公園で、南アパラチア山脈に位置する。面積は522,427エーカー（800平方マイル）で、両州にほぼ均等に分かれている。 [1] 2024年のレクリエーション訪問数は1,200万件を超え、全米で最も訪問者の多い国立公園であり続けている。 [1]

標高はエイブラムス・クリーク河口の約875フィートから、園の最高峰クリングマンズ・ドームの6,643フィートまでに及び、6,000フィートを超える峰が16ある。 [1] 稜線は36マイル以上にわたる切れ目のない連峰をなし、その山地は2億〜3億年前に形成されたとされる世界最古級の山脈の一つである。 [2] この標高差は、ジョージア州からメイン州まで縦断するのに相当する気候と生息環境の変化を園内に再現している。 [2]

## 生物多様性とその由来

同規模の温帯地域として類例のない動植物・菌類の多様さを持ち、アメリカで最も[生物多様性](/hubpedia/biodiversity)の高い国立公園とされる。 [2] 記録済みの種は19,000を超え、科学者はさらに8万〜10万種が生息すると推定している。 [2] 原生の樹木は約100種で北米の他のどの国立公園よりも多く、園の約95%が[森林](/hubpedia/forest-area)に覆われ、その約25%は原生林である。 [2]

顕花植物は1,500種以上が確認され、園はサンショウウオの多様性の中心でもある。鳥類は200種以上、哺乳類68種、原生魚類67種、爬虫類39種、両生類43種が生息する。 [2] アパラチア山系が南北に走っているため、約1万年前の最終氷期に[氷河](/hubpedia/glacier)によって北方の故郷を追われた多くの動植物の避難場所にもなった。 [2]

成育条件を支えるのは雨量と湿度である。年平均雨量は谷間の約55インチから峰の85インチ超まであり、生育期の相対湿度はロッキー山脈地域の約2倍に達する。 [2] 1998年には全生物を対象とする園全域の目録調査であるATBI（全分類群生物多様性目録）が始まり、非営利団体ディスカバー・ライフ・イン・アメリカが調整役を務めている。これまでに約1万種が園の新記録として発見され、そのうち約1,000種は世界初の記録であり、ATBIはアメリカ最大、世界でも有数の継続的自然誌目録に成長した。 [2] この特異な多様性が、1976年10月26日の国際生物圏保護区と1983年12月6日の世界遺産という指定につながった。 [2]

## 成立の経緯

[イエローストーン](/hubpedia/yellowstone)をはじめとする西部の古い国立公園が政府所有地から切り出されたのとは違い、この地は数百の小規模農家と一握りの大手木材・製紙会社が所有していた。 [3] 山に国立公園をという構想は1890年代後半に始まり、ノースカロライナ州議会にも法案が提出されたが成立しなかった。 [3] 1920年代半ば、テネシー州ノックスビルとノースカロライナ州アシュビルを拠点とする支援者たちの努力が実り始め、意外にも自動車愛好家、主にAAAの各自動車クラブが最大の推進役になった。 [3]

1926年5月、カルビン・クーリッジ大統領が署名した法案は、15万エーカーの土地購入を条件にグレートスモーキー山脈とシェナンドーの国立公園設置を定めた。 [3] 政府は国立公園の用地を買うことができなかったため、支援者は募金活動に転じた。両州議会が各200万ドルを拠出し、個人や団体、小遣いを差し出した学童たちの募金もあって1928年までに計500万ドルが集まり、ローラ・スペルマン・ロックフェラー記念基金が同額の500万ドルを上乗せして残りの購入を確実にした。 [3] 一方で多くの家族が住み慣れた家を離れることになり、高齢や病気で移れない人には終身の借地権が認められた。 [3]

初代園長は1931年に着任し、1934年までに両州から30万エーカーの地券が連邦政府へ移譲され、議会は公共施設の本格開発を承認した。 [3] 初期の施設整備と開拓者の建物の修復の多くは、大恐慌期に失業した若者へ仕事と賃金を供するために創設された市民保全部隊（CCC）が1933年から1942年まで担い、園の歩道、キャンプ場、石造りの橋や建物の多くは彼らの仕事である。 [3] 1940年9月2日、フランクリン・D・ルーズベルト大統領がテネシー・ノースカロライナ州境にまたがるニューファウンド・ギャップのロックフェラー記念碑から演説し、公園は「人民の永遠の楽しみのために」奉献された。 [3]

## アメリカクロクマ

園はアメリカ東部でクロクマが生きる最大級の保護地域の一つで、クマは園内のあらゆる標高に生息する。個体数は変動するものの、生物学者は約1,900頭が園内に暮らすと推定し、1平方マイルあたり約2頭という全米最高密度の個体群である。 [4] 20世紀初頭には、生息地の喪失と無規制の狩猟のため、アメリカ大陸のクマはほぼ根絶寸前だった。 [4]

クロクマは雑食で、食性の約85%は植物材料が占める。この地方では珍しく、スモーキーのクマの多くは立ち枯れの樹洞の高所に巣穴を作り、小哺乳類のような「真の冬眠」ではなく、より軽いトーパーという状態で冬を過ごす。 [4] 人との摩擦もある。過去10年で年平均339件の人熊トラブルが報告されており、報告されない例も多い。 [4]

## 利用と管理の現在

公園は周辺経済の核でもあり、2023年には22億ドル超を生み出し、33,748人の雇用を支えた。 [1] 歩道は848マイル（150路線）あり、そのうち74マイルはアパラチアン・トレイルが園内を通る。 [1] 道路は384マイルあり、うち238マイルが舗装、146マイルが未舗装で、トンネル6本、景観橋146、展望地70か所を数える。 [1]

管理対象の構造物は342棟あり、そのうち123棟が歴史的建造物である。かつての住人たちの名残として146の家族墓地に4,847基の墓碑が残り、記録資料は90万件、渓流は2,900マイルに及ぶ。 [1]

## 出典

1. [Park Statistics — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/management/statistics.htm)
2. [Nature & Science — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/nature/index.htm)
3. [Stories — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/historyculture/stories.htm)
4. [Black Bears — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/nature/black-bears.htm)

en.title: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
en.summary: Great Smoky Mountains National Park is a United States national park straddling the North Carolina-Tennessee border in the southern Appalachians. It is the country's most visited and most biologically diverse national park, a World Heritage Site and International Biosphere Reserve set in one of the world's oldest mountain ranges.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Overview and terrain

Great Smoky Mountains National Park is a United States national park straddling the border between North Carolina and Tennessee, set in the southern Appalachian Mountains. It covers 522,427 acres (800 square miles), divided almost evenly between the two states. [1] More than 12 million recreational visits were recorded in 2024, making it consistently the most visited national park in the country. [1]

Elevations run from about 875 feet at the mouth of Abrams Creek to 6,643 feet at Clingmans Dome, the park's highest point, and sixteen peaks rise above 6,000 feet. [1] The crest forms an unbroken chain of peaks for over 36 miles, and the Smokies are one of the oldest mountain ranges in the world, formed perhaps 200-300 million years ago. [2] That range in altitude reproduces within the park the climate and habitat changes a traveler would otherwise see driving from Georgia to Maine. [2]

## Biodiversity and its origins

No other area of equal size in a temperate climate can match the park's variety of animals, plants, fungi, and other organisms — its [biodiversity](/hubpedia/biodiversity) makes it the most biologically diverse national park in the United States. [2] Over 19,000 species have been documented, and scientists believe another 80,000-100,000 species may live here. [2] Some 100 species of native trees find homes in the Smokies, more than in any other North American national park; almost 95% of the park is [forested](/hubpedia/forest-area), and about a quarter of that area is old-growth forest. [2]

Over 1,500 flowering plant species have been identified, and the park is the center of diversity for salamanders. It is home to more than 200 species of birds, 68 mammals, 67 native fish, 39 reptiles, and 43 amphibians. [2] Because the Appalachian chain runs north-south, the Smokies also became a refuge for many species driven from their northern homes by [glaciers](/hubpedia/glacier) in the last ice age around 10,000 years ago. [2]

Rainfall and humidity sustain the growth. Average annual rainfall varies from about 55 inches in the valleys to over 85 inches on some peaks, and relative humidity during the growing season is about twice that of the Rocky Mountain region. [2] In 1998 the Smokies began a park-wide inventory of all life forms, the All Taxa Biodiversity Inventory (ATBI), coordinated by the non-profit partner Discover Life in America. Nearly 10,000 species have since been recorded in the park for the first time, about 1,000 of them new to science, and the ATBI has grown into the largest sustained natural-history inventory in the United States and one of the largest in the world. [2] That extraordinary diversity led to the park's designation as an International Biosphere Reserve on October 26, 1976 and a World Heritage Site on December 6, 1983. [2]

## Establishment

Where older western parks such as [Yellowstone](/hubpedia/yellowstone) were simply carved out of government land, the ground here belonged to hundreds of small farmers and a handful of large timber and paper companies. [3] The idea of a national park in these mountains began in the late 1890s; a bill even entered the North Carolina Legislature, but failed. [3] In the mid-1920s the push finally succeeded, driven by supporters based in Knoxville, Tennessee and Asheville, North Carolina — and, surprisingly, by motorists, mostly the newly formed AAA auto clubs that wanted scenic roads to drive. [3]

In May 1926, President Calvin Coolidge signed a bill providing for the establishment of Great Smoky Mountains and Shenandoah national parks once 150,000 acres of land had been purchased. [3] Since the government could not buy the land itself, supporters turned to fundraising: the two state legislatures appropriated $2 million each, individuals, private groups, and even schoolchildren pledging pennies brought the total to $5 million by 1928, and the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Fund matched it with another $5 million. [3] Many families, however, had to leave their homes; lifetime leases allowed some to stay temporarily, particularly those too old or too sick to move. [3]

The first superintendent arrived in 1931, and by 1934 the states had transferred deeds for 300,000 acres to the federal government, so Congress authorized full development of public facilities. [3] Much of the early development and the restoration of settlers' buildings was done by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), a Depression-era agency created to give work and wages to unemployed young men, which worked in the park from 1933 until 1942; many of the trails, campgrounds, and stone bridges and buildings are its work. [3] On September 2, 1940, President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the park "for the permanent enjoyment of the people," speaking from the Rockefeller Memorial at Newfound Gap astride the Tennessee-North Carolina state line. [3]

## Black bears

The park is one of the largest protected areas in the eastern United States where black bears live, and bears inhabit all of its elevations. Though populations vary, biologists estimate that roughly 1,900 bears live here — a density of about two bears per square mile, the densest black-bear population in the country. [4] By the early 1900s, however, habitat loss and unregulated hunting had nearly eliminated bear populations in the continental US. [4]

Black bears are omnivores, and roughly 85% of their diet consists of plant materials. In a behavior rarely seen elsewhere, many Smokies bears den high above the ground in standing hollow trees, and rather than true hibernation they enter torpor, a lighter and less intense state. [4] Conflict with people occurs as well: an average of 339 negative human-bear encounters have been reported annually over the last ten years, and many more go unreported. [4]

## Use and management today

The park is also an economic hub for the surrounding region, generating over $2.2 billion in 2023 and supporting 33,748 jobs in surrounding communities. [1] Trails run 848 miles across 150 routes, including 74 miles of the Appalachian Trail through the park. [1] Roads total 384 miles — 238 paved and 146 unpaved — with 6 tunnels, 146 scenic bridges, and 70 scenic overlooks. [1]

The park maintains 342 structures, 123 of them historic. Reminders of the former residents remain in 146 family cemeteries with 4,847 gravestones, alongside 900,000 archival records and 2,900 miles of streams. [1]

## 出典

1. [Park Statistics — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/management/statistics.htm)
2. [Nature & Science — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/nature/index.htm)
3. [Stories — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/historyculture/stories.htm)
4. [Black Bears — Great Smoky Mountains National Park](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/nature/black-bears.htm)

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## ポリジェニックリスクスコアとは

ポリジェニックリスクスコア（PRS）は、ゲノム情報だけを用いて、人が特定の医学的状態を持つ、または将来発症する可能性を評価する指標である。個人のPRSは複数のゲノムバリアントの有無に基づく統計的な計算であり、環境など他の要因は考慮に入れない。疾患に関連する変化の総数に基づいて、人が疾患を発症するリスクを知る一つの方法として説明される。 [1][2]

前提として、ヒトは推定60億文字の[ゲノム](/hubpedia/genome)コードにわたってほぼ同一の[DNA](/hubpedia/dna)配列を持つ一方、個人のゲノムにはおよそ400万〜500万のゲノムバリアントが存在する。バリアントの一部は疾患リスクを高め、別の一部はリスクを低下させ、その他はリスクに影響を与えない。 [1]

## 単一遺伝子疾患と複合疾患

遺伝性疾患は、単一の[遺伝子](/hubpedia/gene)に関連するものと、複数の遺伝子と環境要因に影響されるものの2つのクラスに分けられることが多く、多くの疾患はこの両極の間のスペクトラム上にある。単一遺伝子疾患の例として、長期の肺感染と呼吸能力の低下を起こす進行性の遺伝性疾患である嚢胞性線維症は、CFTR遺伝子のバリアントによって引き起こされる。 [1]

対して複合疾患は、多数のゲノムバリアントと食事・睡眠・ストレス・喫煙などの環境影響が組み合わさって生じ、「多くの」を意味するpolyと「遺伝子に関わる」を意味するgenicから、ポリジェニック疾患とも呼ばれる。冠動脈疾患は複合疾患の一つで、患者に頻度の高い約60個のバリアントが見つかっているが、その多くは特定の[染色体](/hubpedia/chromosome)に集まらずゲノム全体に散在する。 [1]

## スコアの計算

研究者は、疾患のある人とない人のゲノムを比較して複合疾患に関連するバリアントを特定し、一つの疾患につき数百から数千のバリアントが使われることがある。その情報をコンピュータに入れて統計を用い、個人のバリアントの集合が特定の疾患のリスクにどう影響するかを推定する。こうした計算は、その疾患に関わる具体的な遺伝子を知らなくても行うことができる。 [1]

背後にある研究手法はゲノムワイド関連解析（GWAS）で、疾患や形質のリスクと統計的に関連するゲノムバリアントを同定するため、多数の人のゲノムを調べて、疾患や形質を持つ群でより頻繁に現れるバリアントを探す。GWASの結果はNHGRI-EBI GWASカタログに集約され、その手法と成果はポリジェニックリスクスコアのアプローチにも応用されている。 [3]

## スコアの解釈

PRSは相対リスクのみを説明し、異なる遺伝的構成を持つ他者と比べた位置を示すが、疾患進行の基準や時間枠は与えない。同じ高スコアでも、22歳の人と98歳の人では生涯リスクが異なり、スコアは因果ではなく相関のみを示す。 [1]

対照的に絶対リスクは疾患の発生する尤度を示し、BRCA1変異を持つ女性の乳がんの60〜80パーセントのような値がこれにあたる。各スコアはベルカーブ分布に置け、多くの人は平均リスクを示す中央に、一部は低リスクまたは高リスクの裾に位置する。有害バリアントを多数持つ人は、偶然によりリスク分布の上位1パーセント、さらには1,000分の1や10,000分の1に入ることがある。高リスク側の領域に位置する人は、このリスクについて医師や遺伝カウンセラーと議論し、さらなる健康評価を受けることで恩恵を受けうるとされる。 [1][2]

## 適用範囲と限界

これまでのゲノム研究の大半は欧州系祖先の個人を対象としており、他の集団のバリアントについてスコアを計算する十分なデータがない可能性がある。現時点ではスコアの精度は欧州系集団でのみ有効かつ有用とされ、他の集団で有用なものにするにはさらなる研究が必要とされる。 [1]

PRSは診療指針がなく生成方法も改良途中のため、医療専門家による日常的利用はまだ始まっていないが、民間医療や消費者直販の企業はすでに消費者向けにスコアを生成している。スコアは常に確実ではなく確率として残る。疾患予測の一因子にすぎない一方で、高リスクの個人が早期兆候のより頻繁な検査や予防的な生活様式の変更から恩恵を受けうると研究者は見ており、PRSの利用法への理解が進めば、より広い利用が見込まれるとされる。 [1][2]

## 出典

1. [Polygenic risk scores](https://www.genome.gov/Health/Genomics-and-Medicine/Polygenic-risk-scores)
2. [Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Polygenic-Risk-Score-PRS)
3. [Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Genome-Wide-Association-Studies)

en.title: Polygenic risk score
en.summary: A polygenic risk score (PRS) is a measure that uses genomic information alone to assess a person's chances of having or developing a particular medical condition, calculated statistically from the presence or absence of multiple genomic variants without taking environmental factors into account. It shows only relative rather than absolute risk, its accuracy may currently be limited to European ancestry populations, and health professionals do not yet use it routinely.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## What is a polygenic risk score?

A polygenic risk score (PRS) is a measure that uses genomic information alone to assess a person's chances of having or developing a particular medical condition. An individual's PRS is a statistical calculation based on the presence or absence of multiple genomic variants, without taking environmental or other factors into account. It is described as one way for people to learn about their risk of developing a disease, based on the total number of changes related to the disease. [1][2]

As background, all humans have near-identical [DNA](/hubpedia/dna) sequences across the estimated 6 billion-letter code of their [genome](/hubpedia/genome), yet roughly 4 to 5 million genomic variants exist in an individual's genome. Some variants increase the risk of developing diseases, others may reduce such risk, and still others have no effect on disease risk. [1]

## Single-gene and complex diseases

Researchers often divide genetic diseases into two classes: those associated with a single [gene](/hubpedia/gene) and those influenced by multiple genes and environmental factors, and many diseases fall on a spectrum between these two extremes. As an example of a single-gene disease, cystic fibrosis, a progressive genetic disease that causes long-term lung infections and limits the ability to breathe over time, is caused by variants in the CFTR gene. [1]

Complex diseases, by contrast, occur as a result of many genomic variants paired with environmental influences such as diet, sleep, stress and smoking, and are also called polygenic diseases, with "poly" meaning many and "genic" involving genes. Coronary artery disease is a complex disease: researchers have found about 60 genomic variants that are present more frequently in people with the disease, most of them dispersed across the genome rather than clustered on one specific [chromosome](/hubpedia/chromosome). [1]

## Calculating the score

Researchers identify genomic variants associated with complex diseases by comparing the genomes of individuals with and without those diseases, and there can be hundreds or even thousands of variants per disease. The information is put into a computer and statistics are used to estimate how the collection of a person's variants affects their risk for a certain disease. All of this can be done without knowing the specific genes involved in the complex disease. [1]

The underlying research approach is the genome-wide association study (GWAS), which surveys the genomes of many people to identify genomic variants statistically associated with a risk for a disease or a particular trait, looking for variants that occur more frequently in those with a specific disease or trait than in those without it. Results from GWAS have been curated in the NHGRI-EBI GWAS catalog, and its methods and results have informed polygenic risk score approaches. [3]

## Interpreting the score

A polygenic risk score can only explain the relative risk for a disease: it shows how a person's risk compares to others with a different genetic constitution, but provides no baseline or timeframe for the progression of a disease. Two people with the same high score for coronary heart disease, one 22 years old and the other 98, will have different lifetime risks of the disease, and polygenic risk scores only show correlations, not causations. [1]

Absolute risk is different: it shows the likelihood of a disease occurring, as in the 60-80% absolute risk of breast cancer for women who carry a BRCA1 mutation. Each polygenic risk score can be put on a bell curve distribution, where most people find their scores in the middle indicating average risk, while others find themselves on the tail ends at either low or high risk. Just by the play of chance, some people carry a large number of harmful variants that can put them in the top 1% or even the top 1/1,000 or 1/10,000 of risk. People with scores on the high-risk portion of the spectrum may benefit from discussions about this risk with their physicians and genetic counselors for further health assessments. [1][2]

## Scope and limitations

The majority of genomic studies to date have examined individuals of European ancestry, so there may not be adequate data about genomic variants from other populations for calculating a polygenic risk score in those populations. At this point in time, the accuracy of polygenic risk scores may only be valid and useful for European ancestry populations, and more research is needed to derive the data for making the scores useful for other populations. [1]

Polygenic risk scores are not yet routinely used by health professionals because there are no guidelines for practice and researchers are still improving how the scores are generated, though private healthcare and direct-to-consumer companies have already begun generating them for consumers. The scores will always be probabilities, not certainties. They are only one factor in predicting disease, but researchers see that high-risk individuals may do better if tested more frequently for early signs of disease or if they adopt lifestyle changes early on, and as scientists learn more about using PRS, such scores may come into wider use. [1][2]

## 出典

1. [Polygenic risk scores](https://www.genome.gov/Health/Genomics-and-Medicine/Polygenic-risk-scores)
2. [Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Polygenic-Risk-Score-PRS)
3. [Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Genome-Wide-Association-Studies)

articles.description: 一塩基多型（SNP、スニップと発音される）は、DNAの単一塩基位置におけるゲノムバリアントであり、ヒト集団の少なくとも1%に存在する一塩基差を指す。ゲノム全体に数百万か所存在し、疾患や形質との関連を調べる目印として大規模な比較研究に使われる。多くは健康に影響しないが、一部は身体的特徴や疾患リスク、薬への反応に関わる。
articles.title: 一塩基多型
articles.summary: 一塩基多型（SNP、スニップと発音される）は、DNAの単一塩基位置におけるゲノムバリアントであり、ヒト集団の少なくとも1%に存在する一塩基差を指す。ゲノム全体に数百万か所存在し、疾患や形質との関連を調べる目印として大規模な比較研究に使われる。多くは健康に影響しないが、一部は身体的特徴や疾患リスク、薬への反応に関わる。
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 一塩基多型の定義

一塩基多型（SNP、「スニップ」と発音される）は、[DNA](/hubpedia/dna)の単一塩基位置におけるゲノムバリアントであり、ある人の[ゲノム](/hubpedia/genome)が別のゲノム配列と1文字だけ異なる場所を指す。より広い枠組みとして、ゲノム学では特定のDNA配列について2つ以上のバリアント型が異なる個人や集団の間に存在する状態をポリモーフィズム（多型）と呼び、その最も一般的な型が一塩基での変異、すなわちSNPである。他の多型は、より長いDNAの範囲に及ぶこともある。 [1][3]

最小のゲノムバリアントは一塩基バリアント（SNV）であり、各SNVは1ヌクレオチドの差を反映する。例えば、あるSNVについて、そのゲノム位置のDNA文字がある人ではCだが別の人ではTという違いになりうる。SNVは最も一般的な[遺伝的変異](/hubpedia/genetic-variation)の型であり、SNPはそのサブタイプにあたる。SNPとみなされるにはSNVがヒト集団の少なくとも1%に存在する必要があり、SNVはSNPのような比較的頻度の高いものと稀な一塩基差の両方を含む、より一般的な用語である。 [2]

## ゲノム内での分布と頻度

[ヒトゲノムプロジェクト](/hubpedia/human-genome-project)によって、遺伝コードにおける1文字の変化がゲノム全体に散らばっていることが分かった。こうした変化のパターンは、個人の間でも集団の間でも異なることが観察されている。 [1]

頻度で見ると、2人のゲノムの間には平均して約1,300塩基ごとに1つの一塩基差が存在する。任意の2人のゲノムは「99.9%同一」とよく言われるが、これは一塩基差だけを数えた単純化であり、実際には平均して99.6%が同一で0.4%が異なる。典型的なゲノムは参照配列と比較して約500万のSNVを持つと推定され、これらは約500万ヌクレオチドに関わる。 [2]

## 研究における役割

科学者はSNPが健康、疾患、薬物応答、その他の形質に影響するかどうか、またどのように影響するかを研究している。ただし大半のゲノムバリアントはゲノムの機能に影響を与えず、影響を持つのは小さな一部である。影響を持つバリアントには、眼の色や身長のような身体的特徴に関わるものや、健康状態、特定の薬への反応の仕方に関わるものがある。 [1][2]

複合疾患を対象とした研究では、例えば糖尿病を持つ数千人と持たない数千人を集めてSNPパターンを比較する。十分な人数が集まれば、患者で同じに見えるゲノム領域をSNPを目印として見つけ出し、遺伝的な原因を詳しく探るべき場所を特定できる。 [1]

## バリアントの検出と参照配列

既知のバリアントを多数調べる場合、マイクロアレイと呼ばれる検査は一度に数十万のSNVを検出できる。まだ知られていない可能性のあるバリアントを含めて検出する、より包括的な方法としては[ゲノムシークエンシング](/hubpedia/genome-sequencing)が行われる。 [2]

個人のゲノム配列でバリアントを検出するには通常、比較対象となる既存の参照配列が必要であり、新たに生成された配列は参照ゲノム配列と直接比較されて、両者の全差異がバリアントとして目録化される。単一の参照配列に伴う偏りを減らすため、集団間のゲノム変異をより網羅的に扱うヒトパンゲノムという枠組みも作られている。 [2]

## 健康との関係と用語の境界

ヒトの健康に影響するゲノムバリアントはごく一部にすぎない。嚢胞性線維症や鎌状赤血球症のように疾患を直接引き起こす場合もあれば、高血圧や糖尿病のように、その状態への全体的なリスクに寄与する程度にとどまる場合もある。 [2]

SNPという用語は頻度によって区切られるため、集団内の存在割合が1%に満たない一塩基差はSNPとは呼ばれず、SNVというより広い用語に含められる。こうした頻度に基づく区別により、一般的な差異と稀な差異が用語上で分けて扱われる。 [2]

## 出典

1. [Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Single-Nucleotide-Polymorphisms-SNPs)
2. [Human Genomic Variation](https://www.genome.gov/about-genomics/educational-resources/fact-sheets/human-genomic-variation)
3. [Polymorphism](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Polymorphism)

en.title: Single-nucleotide polymorphism
en.summary: A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP, pronounced "snip") is a genomic variant at a single base position in the DNA, defined as a single-nucleotide difference present in at least 1% of the human population. Millions of them exist across the genome and serve as markers in large comparison studies of disease and traits. Most have no health impact, but some relate to physical characteristics, disease risk or drug response.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Definition of a single-nucleotide polymorphism

A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP, pronounced "snip") is a genomic variant at a single base position in the [DNA](/hubpedia/dna), a one-letter place where a person's [genome](/hubpedia/genome) varies from another genome sequence. In the wider framework, genomics uses the term polymorphism for the presence of two or more variant forms of a specific DNA sequence among different individuals or populations, and the most common type of polymorphism is variation at a single nucleotide — the SNP. Other polymorphisms can involve much longer stretches of DNA. [1][3]

The smallest genomic variants are single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), each reflecting a difference of one nucleotide. For a given SNV, the DNA letter at that genomic position might be a C in one person but a T in another. SNVs are the most common type of [genomic variation](/hubpedia/genetic-variation), and a SNP is a subtype of them: to be considered a SNP, a SNV must be present in at least 1% of the human population, so SNV is the more general term covering both relatively common variants such as SNPs and rare single-nucleotide differences. [2]

## Distribution and frequency across the genome

Thanks to the [Human Genome Project](/hubpedia/human-genome-project), these single-letter changes in the genetic code are known to be placed all across our genomes. The patterns are observed to vary between people and even between populations. [1]

On average, a single-nucleotide difference exists between two people's genomes once every 1,300 nucleotides or so. It is often stated that any two people's genomes are 99.9% identical, but this is an over-simplification that only counts single-nucleotide differences; in reality the two are on average 99.6% identical and 0.4% different. A typical genome is estimated to carry about 5 million SNVs compared with a reference sequence, involving about 5 million nucleotides. [2]

## Role in research

Scientists study if and how SNPs in a genome influence health, disease, drug response and other traits. Most genomic variants, however, have no influence on the functioning of a person's genome; only a small subset has an impact, influencing physical characteristics such as eye color and height, health conditions, or how a person responds to certain medications. [1][2]

In studies of complex diseases, for example, researchers group together thousands of people who have diabetes and compare their SNP patterns to those of thousands who do not. With enough people, the SNPs can be used as markers to find areas of the genome that appear to be the same in people with the disease, indicating where to look in more detail for a genetic cause. [1]

## Detecting variants and reference sequences

When many known variants need to be examined, a test called a microarray can detect hundreds of thousands of SNVs at once. A more comprehensive way to detect genomic variants, including those that might not yet be known, is to perform [genome sequencing](/hubpedia/genome-sequencing). [2]

Detecting variants in a person's genome sequence usually requires an existing sequence for comparison: each newly generated sequence is directly compared to a reference human genome sequence, cataloguing all differences between the two as variants. To reduce biases that can come with a single reference, the human pangenome is a framework that aims to account for genomic variation across human populations more completely. [2]

## Health relevance and the boundaries of the term

Only a small fraction of genomic variants affects human health. In some cases variants directly cause diseases, as in cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease; in others their effects are more subtle, as in hypertension and diabetes, where a variant might contribute to the overall risk a person has of the condition. [2]

Because the term SNP is bounded by frequency, a single-nucleotide difference present in less than 1% of the population is not called a SNP but is included under the broader term SNV. This frequency-based distinction separates common differences from rare ones in the terminology. [2]

## 出典

1. [Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs)](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Single-Nucleotide-Polymorphisms-SNPs)
2. [Human Genomic Variation](https://www.genome.gov/about-genomics/educational-resources/fact-sheets/human-genomic-variation)
3. [Polymorphism](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Polymorphism)

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 希少疾患とは

希少疾患とは、一般に、米国内のある時点で20万人未満の人々に影響する疾患を指す。個別には珍しくても、その種類は6,800を超え、合計すると推定2,500万〜3,000万人の米国人が希少疾患の影響を受けている。 [1]

## 原因

多くの希少疾患について、正確な原因はまだ分かっていない。それでも相当な部分は、単一の[遺伝子](/hubpedia/gene)の変異（変化）にたどることができ、こうした疾患は希少遺伝性疾患と呼ばれる。こうした[遺伝的変異](/hubpedia/genetic-variation)の多くは親から子へ世代を超えて伝わりうるため、特定の希少疾患が家族内で繰り返し現れる理由が説明される。 [1]

ただし遺伝はパズルの一片にすぎず、食事、喫煙、化学物質への曝露のような環境要因も希少疾患で役割を果たしうる。環境要因は直接疾患を引き起こす場合もあれば、遺伝要因と相互作用して疾患を起こしたり重症度を高めたりする場合もある。 [1]

## 単一遺伝子に起因する例

単一遺伝子の変異が原因となる希少疾患の例として、嚢胞性線維症は呼吸器系と消化器系に、ハンチントン病は脳と神経系に、筋ジストロフィーは筋肉に影響する。 [1]

単一遺伝子は、一部の稀な遺伝性のがんタイプの原因でもある。BRCA1遺伝子とBRCA2遺伝子では特定の変異が遺伝性の乳がんと卵巣がんのリスクを高め、FAP遺伝子の変異は遺伝性の結腸がんのリスクを高める。 [1]

## 環境要因に関係する例

環境要因に関係する希少疾患には、ビタミンが不足した食事や特定の薬によって起こる稀なタイプの貧血がある。環境要因による希少がんの例では、胸郭の内側を覆う細胞に影響する中皮腫があり、その症例の90%超は、かつて耐火・断熱材に広く使われた繊維状の鉱物であるアスベストへの曝露が原因とされる。 [1]

## 治療開発と研究

研究者は近年、様々な希少疾患を診断・治療し予防する方法の解明でかなりの進展を遂げたが、大半の希少疾患には治療法がないため、なすべきことはまだ多く残る。1983年の孤児薬法は製薬企業に希少疾患向け治療開発の動機を与え、連邦法として署名されてから25年間で米国食品医薬品局は340を超える希少疾患向け治療を承認した。 [1]

NIHはさらに、希少・顧みられない疾患治療プログラムで新たな治療開発を加速する統合的研究パイプラインを作り、希少疾患の研究を推進するため希少疾患研究イノベーション部門を設置した。診断の側面では、長年診断を逃れてきた病状を対象に、NHGRI、NIH希少疾患研究局、NIH臨床センターが2008年に組織した未診断疾患プログラムが、謎の病気を持つ患者への回答と、希少・一般的疾患の医学知識の前進という2つの目標を追っている。 [1][2]

このプログラムは複数の[ゲノムシークエンシング](/hubpedia/genome-sequencing)技術を使って希少・新規の遺伝的原因を特定しており、これまでに30を超える新たな疾患が発見され、症例の25〜50%が臨床・分子・生化学的いずれかの診断に至っている。患者の診断には、既知疾患の稀な表現型、多系統の複合疾患、これまで同定されたことのない新規疾患が含まれる。 [2]

## 情報と支援

患者と家族にタイムリーで信頼できる情報を届けるため、ORDRとNHGRIは遺伝・希少疾患情報センター（GARD）をオンラインに設置した。GARDは2002年にNHGRIとDRDRIによって創設され、英語とスペイン語の両方で遺伝・希少疾患について最新かつ正確な情報を提供できる経験豊富な情報専門家への、ほぼ24時間のアクセスを提供している。 [1][3]

加えて、様々な希少疾患に関する情報と支援の提供、研究の促進、政策課題の提言を行う非営利団体が多くある。 [1]

## 出典

2. [NIH Undiagnosed Diseases Program (UDP)](https://www.genome.gov/Current-NHGRI-Clinical-Studies/NIH-Undiagnosed-Diseases-Program)
3. [Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center](https://www.genome.gov/For-Patients-and-Families/Genetic-and-Rare-Diseases-Information-Center)

en.title: Rare disease
en.summary: A rare disease is generally considered to be a disease that affects fewer than 200,000 people in the United States at any given time; more than 6,800 are known, together affecting an estimated 25 to 30 million Americans. The exact cause of many remains unknown, though a significant portion can be traced to mutations in a single gene, and environmental factors also play a role. Most have no treatment, and statutory incentives, research infrastructure and genome-sequencing diagnostic programs support the response.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## What is a rare disease?

A rare disease is generally considered to be a disease that affects fewer than 200,000 people in the United States at any given time. Individually uncommon, they number more than 6,800 kinds, and altogether rare diseases affect an estimated 25 million to 30 million Americans. [1]

## Causes

The exact cause of many rare diseases remains unknown. Still, for a significant portion the problem can be traced to mutations (changes) in a single [gene](/hubpedia/gene), and such diseases are referred to as rare, genetic diseases. Many of these [genetic variants](/hubpedia/genetic-variation) can be passed on from one generation to the next, which explains why certain rare diseases run in families. [1]

Genetics, however, is just one piece of the puzzle: environmental factors such as diet, smoking, or exposure to chemicals can also play a role in rare diseases. Such factors may directly cause disease, or interact with genetic factors to cause or increase the severity of disease. [1]

## Examples caused by single genes

Examples of rare diseases caused by mutations in single genes include cystic fibrosis, which affects the respiratory and digestive systems; Huntington's disease, which affects the brain and nervous system; and muscular dystrophies, which affect the muscles. [1]

Single genes are also responsible for some rare, inherited types of cancer. In the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, certain mutations increase the risk for hereditary breast and ovarian cancers, and mutations in the FAP gene increase the risk for hereditary colon cancer. [1]

## Examples related to environmental factors

Rare diseases related to environmental factors include uncommon types of anemia caused by vitamin-deficient diets or certain medications. As an example of an environmentally caused rare cancer, mesothelioma affects the cells lining the chest cavity, and more than 90 percent of its cases are caused by exposure to asbestos, a fibrous mineral once widely used in fireproofing and insulation materials. [1]

## Treatment development and research

Researchers have made considerable progress in recent years in figuring out ways to diagnose, treat and even prevent a variety of rare diseases, yet much more remains to be done because there are no treatments for the vast majority of rare diseases. The Orphan Drug Act of 1983 provides incentives for drug companies to develop treatments for rare diseases, and in the 25 years since the Act was signed into federal law the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved more than 340 treatments for rare diseases. [1]

The NIH further created an integrated research pipeline to jump start the development of new treatments through the Therapeutics for Rare and Neglected Diseases program, and established the Division of Rare Diseases Research Innovation to help advance research focused on rare diseases. On the diagnostic side, the Undiagnosed Diseases Program — organized initially in 2008 by NHGRI, the NIH Office of Rare Diseases Research and the NIH Clinical Center for longstanding conditions that elude diagnosis — pursues two goals: providing answers to patients with mysterious conditions and advancing medical knowledge about rare and common diseases. [1][2]

The program uses multiple [genome sequencing](/hubpedia/genome-sequencing) technologies to identify rare and new genetic causes of disease; so far more than 30 new diseases have been discovered, and 25-50% of cases have been resolved with a clinical, molecular or biochemical diagnosis. Patient diagnoses include uncommon presentations of known disorders, multi-systemic complex disorders, and new disorders that have never been identified. [2]

## Information and support

To provide patients and their families with timely and reliable information, ORDR and NHGRI created the online Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center (GARD). GARD was created in 2002 by NHGRI and DRDRI, and provides immediate, virtually round-the-clock access to experienced information specialists who can furnish current and accurate information — in both English and Spanish — about genetic and rare diseases. [1][3]

In addition, there are many non-profit groups that provide information and support, promote research and advocate for policy issues related to various rare diseases. [1]

## 出典

1. [Rare Diseases FAQ](https://www.genome.gov/FAQ/Rare-Diseases)
2. [NIH Undiagnosed Diseases Program (UDP)](https://www.genome.gov/Current-NHGRI-Clinical-Studies/NIH-Undiagnosed-Diseases-Program)
3. [Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center](https://www.genome.gov/For-Patients-and-Families/Genetic-and-Rare-Diseases-Information-Center)

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 祖先解析とは

遺伝的祖先とは、ある個人が生物学的にその子孫である人々に関する情報を指し、彼らとの遺伝的関係を含む。遺伝情報は歴史情報と組み合わせて、その個人の遠い祖先がどこに住んでいたかを推測するのに使える。個人の[ゲノム](/hubpedia/genome)は、近い祖先も遠い祖先も含めて、祖先の歴史を明らかにする助けとなる。 [1][3]

[ヒトゲノムプロジェクト](/hubpedia/human-genome-project)以降の進歩により、生きている人と長く亡くなった人のゲノム配列を比較し、私たちの集団の祖先史をたどることが可能になった。ヒトゲノムプロジェクトが作り出した参照ヒトゲノム配列は、現在、新たに生成されたゲノム配列と日常的に比較されており、異なる集団で時を経て起きたゲノムの変化を明らかにし、人類の起源と祖先の様々な物語を解読するより強力な方法を提供している。 [3]

## 祖先情報マーカーによる推定

祖先情報マーカー（AIM）は、世界の異なる地理的地域の集団の間で、出現頻度が大きく異なる特定のDNA配列のポリモーフィズムの組である。AIMは個人の祖先の地理的起源を推定するのに使え、通常はアフリカ、アジア、ヨーロッパの大陸単位の起源に整理される。 [2]

AIMはゲノム内で配列が変化している位置であり、それらのマーカーの相対的な多さは、個人が祖先をたどれる大陸によって異なる。20〜30、あるいはそれ以上の一連のマーカーを使って個人をジェノタイピングすれば、それらの頻度から祖先がどこから来たかを推定できる。AIMは、人々が同じ背景を持つかを見る疫学研究や、法医学研究にも使われる。 [2]

## ゲノムが明らかにする人類史

約20年前、骨や毛皮、さらには土壌のような古代試料から微量の[DNA](/hubpedia/dna)を抽出し、高感度な方法で配列を決定する技術が開発された。こうしたゲノム研究により、私たちの祖先であるホモ・サピエンスがネアンデルタールのような類似種と分岐しつつあった約50万年前の人類ゲノムまで調べられるようになった。 [3]

ネアンデルタールは人類とは異なる移動経路をたどったが、そのDNA配列の痕跡は今日の私たちのゲノムに残っている。2017年の研究では、一部の欧州人が概日リズムに影響するネアンデルタール様の配列を今も持ち、朝型か夜型かに関わることが分かった。一方、赤毛につながるMC1R遺伝子の変異はネアンデルタールでは極めて稀か存在しなかったため、その形質はヒト固有と見られる。 [3]

6,000年前から現在までのアフリカ人のゲノム配列決定により、人類が異なる集団に分かれ、複数の時期に世界各地へ移動したことが明らかになった。南部アフリカでは、先住の狩猟採集民、次いで牧畜民が、約2,000年前にバントゥー系の農耕民に置き換わったと見られる。また欧州では、2008年の研究が欧州人の集団で約20万か所のゲノム上の相違位置を調べ、集団間のゲノムバリアントのパターンからヨーロッパの地図を90%の精度で再現できた。さらに新たな欧州人のゲノムを解析すると、その人の出身地を数百km以内で予測でき、米国での最近の研究でも、[遺伝的変異](/hubpedia/genetic-variation)と系譜記録を組み合わせて出生地をかなり正確に推測できることが示されている。 [3]

## 消費者向け祖先検査

特定の集団やグループにおけるゲノム変異の理解が進むにつれ、祖先の出自を解読するためのより頑健な検査が開発されており、ゲノムに基づく祖先検査や家系の系譜歴史を調べられる[遺伝子検査](/hubpedia/genetic-testing)の商業サービスは多くある。ただし、こうした検査の結果は、家族史や自分自身についての認識を変える可能性がある。 [3]

## 祖先検査がもたらす影響と限界

祖先検査では、祖先の出自が思っていたものと違うと判明する人や、近い親族が思っていた人と違ったと分かる人がいる。養子となった子どもがDNA検査で実の親や、それまで知らなかった兄弟姉妹を探すこともある。国によっては、研究により1〜10%の子どもが、実は生物学上の父でない人を実父と思って育てられていると報告されている。祖先検査は繊細で複雑な状況をもたらしうるため、こうした検査を使う前に起こりうる結果を考えておくことが重要とされる。 [3]

## 出典

1. [Genetic Ancestry](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Genetic-Ancestry)
2. [Ancestry-informative Markers](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Ancestry-informative-Markers)
3. [Human Origins and Ancestry](https://www.genome.gov/dna-day/15-ways/human-origins-ancestry)

en.title: Ancestry analysis
en.summary: Ancestry analysis is the study of genetic ancestry — information about the people an individual is biologically descended from. Through ancestry-informative markers and comparison with reference genomes it can estimate geographical origins by continent and reconstruct human migration history, while ancient DNA analysis reveals our relationship with Neanderthals. Consumer testing is widely available, but it can produce delicate results that alter perceptions of family.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## What is genetic ancestry?

Genetic ancestry refers to information about the people that an individual is biologically descended from, including their genetic relationships. Genetic information can be combined with historical information to infer where an individual's distant ancestors lived. Your [genome](/hubpedia/genome) helps uncover the history of your ancestors, both near and distant. [1][3]

Advances since the [Human Genome Project](/hubpedia/human-genome-project) allow us to compare genome sequences among humans, living and long-deceased, and to trace our collective ancestral history. The reference human genome sequence the project produced is now regularly used for comparison with newly generated genome sequences, revealing genomic changes that have occurred in different populations over time and providing a more powerful way to decipher the various stories of human origins and ancestry. [3]

## Estimation with ancestry-informative markers

Ancestry-informative markers (AIMs) are sets of polymorphisms for a particular DNA sequence that appear in substantially different frequencies between populations from different geographical regions of the world. They can be used to estimate the geographical origins of an individual's ancestors, typically by continent of origin: Africa, Asia, or Europe. [2]

AIMs are locations in the genome that have varied sequences, and the relative abundance of those markers differs based on the continent from which individuals can trace their ancestry. Using a series of these markers — sometimes 20 or 30 or more — and genotyping an individual, the frequency of the markers can indicate where their ancestors may have come from. AIMs are used in epidemiological studies to see whether people have the same background, and sometimes in forensic studies as well. [2]

## Human history revealed by the genome

About 20 years ago, scientists developed techniques for extracting small amounts of [DNA](/hubpedia/dna) from ancient samples, like bones or fur or even soil, and used very sensitive methods for sequencing it. Studies like these have allowed us to examine human genomes from around 500,000 years ago, when our ancestors — the species Homo sapiens — were diverging from other similar species such as the Neanderthals. [3]

Neanderthals took a different path than humans in their migrations around the world, but traces of Neanderthal DNA sequences remain in our genomes today. A 2017 study found that some Europeans still carry Neanderthal-like sequences that influence their circadian rhythms, making them more likely to be a morning person or a night owl. In contrast, variations in the MC1R gene that lead to red hair were extremely rare or nonexistent in Neanderthals, so that trait seems to be human-specific. [3]

Genome sequencing of Africans living in different times — from as long as 6,000 years ago to today — has revealed that humans divided into different groups and moved around the world at multiple times. In Southern Africa, local hunter-gatherers and then herders appear to have been replaced by Bantu farmers around 2,000 years ago. In Europe, a 2008 study looked at about 200,000 specific places in the human genome where people differ from each other among a collection of Europeans, and the patterns of genomic variants among groups could be used to reproduce the map of Europe with 90 percent accuracy. When a new European person's genome was analyzed, researchers could predict where that person was from within a few hundred kilometers, and more recent studies in the United States show that [genomic variation](/hubpedia/genetic-variation) coupled with genealogical records can be used to infer birth location quite accurately. [3]

## Consumer ancestry testing

As we learn more about genomic variation in specific populations and groups, more robust tests are being developed to help decipher ancestral origins, and there are many commercial [genetic testing](/hubpedia/genetic-testing) services that allow you to purchase a genomics-based ancestry test or explore your family's genealogical history. But the results of these tests may alter your perception of your family history and even of yourself. [3]

## Consequences and limits of ancestry testing

With such testing, some people have discovered that their ancestral origin is not what they thought, while others have found that close relatives are not who they thought. Some adopted children have used DNA tests to track down their birth parents, or to find previously unknown siblings. Some studies report that, depending on the country, anywhere between 1 percent and 10 percent of children are raised thinking that someone is their biological father when, in fact, that person is not. Ancestry testing can lead to delicate and complex situations, so it is important to think about the potential consequences before using such tests. [3]

## 出典

1. [Genetic Ancestry](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Genetic-Ancestry)
2. [Ancestry-informative Markers](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Ancestry-informative-Markers)
3. [Human Origins and Ancestry](https://www.genome.gov/dna-day/15-ways/human-origins-ancestry)

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 家系図とは

家系図（ペディグリー）とは、遺伝学において、形質や健康状態が家族の世代を通じてどう受け継がれるかを図式化する表である。家系図は特に家族成員間の関係を示し、情報が得られる場合には、関心のある形質を持つ個人を示す。 [1]

家系図は、家族の異なる成員とそのつながりを描く地図であり、グラフである。親、兄弟姉妹、いとこといった、誰がどうつながっているかという関係を目視で把握できるようにする。家系図はまた、形質や状態が世代を通じてどう伝わりうるか、何がそれに伴いうるかを判断する助けにもなる。 [1]

## 家族歴と家系図

医学における家族歴とは、個人と、その人の生存・死去を問わない生物学上の家族成員の疾患と健康状態の記録である。家族歴は、ある人が特定の疾患、障害、状態を持つ、あるいは発症する遺伝的リスクが高まっているかを判断する助けになる。そして家族歴はしばしば、個人間の関係を示す家系図（家族の木）を描いて記録される。 [2]

## 遺伝形式の読み取り

家系図を通じて記録された家族歴は、医療チームが遺伝とリスクを理解する助けとなる。例えば、ある疾患がすべての世代に現れる場合、その疾患は優性遺伝されるとみなされる。別の家族では、疾患が毎世代には存在せず、潜性（劣性）遺伝として現れたり、多因子のパターンをたどったりすることがある。正確で詳細な家族歴を記録すれば、家族における疾患の性質だけでなく、記録されたパターンに基づく重症度や誰が影響を受けるかのリスクについても、医療チームが洞察を得られる可能性がある。 [2]

## 医療現場での使われ方

医療現場では、遺伝的に近い家族成員について3世代の家族歴を取る。その第一の目標は生物学上の家族内の疾患をスクリーニングすることであり、第二の目標は、潜在する問題を示しうる健康状態の遺伝パターン、すなわち優性形質、性連鎖パターン、潜性[遺伝子](/hubpedia/gene)を特定することである。 [3]

家族歴における危険信号としては、同じ問題を持つ複数の家族成員、予想より早い時期の発症、あまり罹患しない性別での疾患（男性の乳がんなど）、突然死、民族性、近親婚（近い血縁者同士の子どもにおける[潜性疾患リスク](/hubpedia/carrier-screening)の判断など）、早期または反復性の妊娠喪失が挙げられる。こうした評価は、さらなるゲノム解析の対象となる人の優先順位づけや、一次・二次予防の必要性が高い人を特定するのに使われる。 [3]

## 検査と専門家への接続

危険信号が見つかった後の[遺伝子検査](/hubpedia/genetic-testing)は、目的と型によって分類される。検査の理由には、疑わしい疾患のための診断検査、個人が疾患を発症するリスクにあるかを調べる予測検査、予防的治療の必要性を見極めるスクリーニングという3つの広い区分があり、検査には遺伝子、[染色体](/hubpedia/chromosome)、タンパク質の解析が含まれる。 [3]

また、遺伝カウンセラーや臨床遺伝医のような遺伝の専門家への相談依頼や紹介も行われ、そこでは家族歴と遺伝リスクについての議論や、検査前後の情報提供を含む追加の評価と管理が行われる。 [3]

## 家族が作る家系図

NHGRIと米国衛生総監の家族史イニシアティブが作ったMy Family Health Portraitは、自分自身の家族健康歴を作成するのを助けるウェブサイトである。利用者は健康情報を入力して、家族の木の図と家族健康歴の表を作り、その表と図は印刷して家族成員や医師と共有できる。両親、祖父母、その他の血縁者が患った病気をたどることは、医師がその人がリスクを持ちうる疾患を予測する助けになる。 [4]

2004年11月、家族が集まる感謝祭に合わせて、米国衛生総監リチャード・カルモナと保健社会福祉省は、米国衛生総監の家族史イニシアティブと呼ばれる全国公衆衛生キャンペーンを開始した。キャンペーンは家族健康歴の重要性に注目を集めるもので、その一環としてパソコンで使うダウンロード型ツールが公開され、1年後の2005年11月にはWebベースのツールが公開された。 [4]

## 家系図の限界と維持

家系図は、形質に関する情報が得られる場合にのみ、その情報を示すことができる。また洞察を得られるのは正確で詳細な家族歴が記録された場合であり、医療現場では患者や家族と協力しながら家族歴を維持し更新し続けることが行われる。 [1][2][3]

en.title: Pedigree
en.summary: A pedigree, as related to genetics, is a chart that diagrams the inheritance of a trait or health condition through generations of a family, showing the relationships among family members and, when the information is available, which individuals have a trait of interest. It is used to distinguish dominant, recessive and multifactorial patterns, and in medicine a three-generation family history is screened for red flags. Tools for families to build their own are also provided.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## What is a pedigree?

A pedigree, as related to genetics, is a chart that diagrams the inheritance of a trait or health condition through generations of a family. It particularly shows the relationships among family members and, when the information is available, indicates which individuals have a trait of interest. [1]

A pedigree is a map that depicts the different members of a family and their connections — a graph that makes assessing who is connected and their relationships, such as parent, sibling or cousin, apparent by visual inspection. A pedigree can also help determine how a trait or condition might be passed down through the generations and what might accompany it. [1]

## Family history and the pedigree

A family history, as related to medicine, is a record of the diseases and health conditions of an individual and that person's biological family members, both living and deceased. A family history can help determine whether someone has an increased genetic risk of having or developing certain diseases, disorders or conditions. It is often recorded by drawing a pedigree — a family tree — that illustrates the relationships among individuals. [2]

## Reading inheritance patterns

The family history recorded through a pedigree helps medical teams understand inheritance and risk. For example, certain disorders can show in every generation, in which case the disorder would be dominantly inherited; in other families a disorder may not be present in every generation and may appear as a recessive inheritance, or even follow a multifactorial pattern. Recording an accurate and detailed family history can allow medical teams to gain insights not only into the nature of the condition in a given family, but possibly the severity and risks of who is affected based on the pattern noted. [2]

## How it is used in clinical practice

In clinical practice, a three-generation family history is taken for genetically related family members. The first goal is to screen for diseases within the biological family, and the second goal is to identify patterns of inheritance for health conditions that may indicate a potential problem — dominant traits, sex-linked patterns and recessive [genes](/hubpedia/gene). [3]

Red flags in the family history include multiple family members with the same problem, earlier onset of disease than might be expected, disease in the less commonly affected biological sex (such as breast cancer in men), sudden deaths, ethnicity, consanguinity (used to determine the risk of recessive disease in offspring of closely related individuals, an area related to [carrier screening](/hubpedia/carrier-screening)), and early or recurrent pregnancy loss. Such assessment is used to prioritize individuals for possible further genomic analysis, and to identify those at increased need for primary and secondary prevention. [3]

## Connecting to testing and specialists

When red flags are found, the [genetic testing](/hubpedia/genetic-testing) that follows is categorized according to purpose and type. Reasons for testing include three broad categories — diagnostic testing for a suspected condition, predictive testing to determine if an individual is at risk of developing a condition, and screening to identify the need for preventive therapy — and the tests include analyses of genes, [chromosomes](/hubpedia/chromosome), or proteins. [3]

Consultation with, or referral to, genetic specialists such as genetic counselors and clinical geneticists also takes place, involving further workup and management that includes discussing family history and genetic risk and providing information before or after testing. [3]

## Pedigrees built by families

My Family Health Portrait, a product of NHGRI and the U.S. Surgeon General's Family History Initiative, is a website that helps you create your own family health history. Users provide their health information to build a drawing of their family tree and a chart of their family health history, and both the chart and the drawing can be printed and shared with family members and a doctor. Tracing the illnesses suffered by parents, grandparents and other blood relatives can help a doctor predict the disorders to which a person may be at risk. [4]

In November 2004 — timed to coincide with Thanksgiving, when families traditionally gather — U.S. Surgeon General Richard H. Carmona and the Department of Health and Human Services launched a national public health campaign called the U.S. Surgeon General's Family History Initiative. The campaign focused attention on the importance of the family health history, launching a downloadable tool for personal computers, and one year later, in November 2005, the Web-based tool followed. [4]

## Limits and upkeep of a pedigree

A pedigree can only indicate trait information when that information is available, and insights depend on an accurate and detailed family history being recorded. In clinical settings, maintaining and updating the family history in collaboration with patients and families is an ongoing task. [1][2][3]

articles.summary: アメリカ独立宣言は、1776年7月4日に大陸会議が採択した、北米13植民地のイギリスからの独立を宣言する文書である。トーマス・ジェファーソンら五人委員会が起草し、8月2日から56名の代表が羊皮紙の謄清本に署名した。宣言はすべての人が平等に造られ、生命・自由・幸福の追求を不可侵の権利として持つと掲げ、国王への訴状を列挙した上で連合植民地の自由と独立を宣告した。
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 概要

アメリカ独立宣言は、1776年7月4日に大陸会議が採択した、北米13植民地のイギリスからの独立を宣言する文書である。宣言は羊皮紙に謄清され、1776年8月2日から代表たちが署名を始めた。 [1]

文書は冒頭で、すべての人は平等に造られ、生命・自由・幸福の追求を含む不可侵の権利を持つという自明の真理を掲げ、続けて連合植民地が自由かつ独立の国家であることを宣告している。 [2]

## 歴史的背景

独立を宣言するリー決議の該当部分が採択されたのは1776年7月2日のことだが、大陸会議はそれに先立つ6月10日に、植民地のための独立声明を起草する五人委員会を既に任命していた。 [1]

## 起草と採択

五人委員会はトーマス・ジェファーソン、ジョン・アダムズ、ベンジャミン・フランクリン、ロバート・R・リビングストン、ロジャー・シャーマンで構成され、実際の執筆はジェファーソンに委ねられた。 [1]

ジェファーソンは6月11日から28日の間に草案を書き上げ、アダムズとフランクリンに示して若干の修正を受けた後、7月2日の独立条項採択を受けて議会へ提出した。議会による修正作業は7月3日終日と7月4日の大半を費やし、宣言は7月4日の午後に採択された。 [1]

## 印刷・謄清と署名

採択された宣言は7月5日、ジェファーソン委員会の監督の下で印刷に付され、印刷本は議長ジョン・ハンコックと書記チャールズ・トムソンの名だけを載せて、各州議会、各種会議、安全委員会、大陸軍の司令官に配布された。 [1]

7月19日、議会は宣言を「十三合衆国の一致の宣言」という新標題で羊皮紙に謄清し、謄清された文書に全議員が署名するよう命じた。謄清とは公文書を大きな字体で書き写す作業で、宣言の謄清者はおそらくトムソンの助手ティモシー・マトロックだったとされる。 [1]

8月2日、議長ハンコックが大胆な署名で謄清本に名を連ね、他の代表は慣例に従って右端から、州を最北のニューハンプシャーから最南のジョージアの順に配して署名した。全員がその日に出席していたわけではなく、最終的に56名の代表が署名し、エルブリッジ・ジェリー、オリバー・ウォルコット、ルイス・モリス、トマス・マッキーン、マシュー・ソーントンは後日の署名となった。起草委員だったリビングストンを含む一部の代表は署名しなかった。 [1]

## 宣言の構成と主張

宣言は「われわれは、これらの真理が自明であると信じる」という一節で始まり、すべての人は平等に造られ、造物主から生命・自由・幸福の追求を含む不可侵の権利を与えられていると述べる。 [2]

続けて宣言は、これらの権利を保障するために政府が人々の間に設立され、その正当な権力は被治者の同意に由来すると主張し、政府がその目的を破壊するものとなった場合、人民にはそれを変革または廃止して新しい政府を樹立する権利があると説く。 [2]

宣言の中ほどは「現在の大不列顛国王の歴史は、これら諸州に絶対的専制を樹立することを直接の目的とする、繰り返しの侵害と簒奪の歴史である」と位置づけ、「公正な世界に事実を提出しよう」として具体的な訴状を列挙する。訴状には、公共の利益に必要な法律への同意拒否、代表議会の度重なる解散、平時の同意なき常備軍の駐留、同意なき課税、陪審裁判の利益の剥奪などが含まれる。 [2]

結びの部分で宣言は、連合植民地は「自由かつ独立の国家であり、またそうあるべき」であり、英国王冠への忠誠をすべて解くと宣告し、自由かつ独立の国家として戦争の遂行、平和の締結、同盟の締結、通商の確立を行う完全な権力を有すると述べた。この宣言を支持するため、署名者たちは「われわれの生命、財産、神聖な名誉」を相互に誓い合った。 [2]

## 展示と後世への影響

国家公文書館が公開する謄写は、パーチメント宣言の石版謄写本（ストーン・エングレービング）に基づくもので、その原本は国家公文書館博物館のロタンダに常設展示されている。 [2]

宣言の原理は後世にも参照され続けた。1863年、エイブラハム・リンカーンは[ゲティスバーグ演説](/hubpedia/gettysburg-address)の中で独立宣言とその自由と平等の原理を明示的に引用している。 [3]

en.title: United States Declaration of Independence
en.summary: The United States Declaration of Independence is the document adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, proclaiming the independence of the thirteen North American colonies from Great Britain. Drafted by a committee of five with the writing delegated to Thomas Jefferson, it was engrossed on parchment and signed by 56 delegates beginning August 2. It declares that all men are created equal with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, lists grievances against the King, and proclaims the colonies free and independent states.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Overview

The United States Declaration of Independence is the document adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, proclaiming the independence of the thirteen North American colonies from Great Britain. It was engrossed on parchment, and delegates began signing it on August 2, 1776. [1]

The document opens by holding certain truths to be self-evident—that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness—and concludes by declaring the united colonies to be free and independent states. [2]

## Historical background

The independence section of the Lee Resolution was not adopted until July 2, 1776, but Congress had already appointed a committee of five on June 10 to draft a statement of independence for the colonies. [1]

## Drafting and adoption

The committee of five consisted of Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston, and Roger Sherman, with the actual writing delegated to Jefferson. [1]

Jefferson drafted the statement between June 11 and 28, submitted drafts to Adams and Franklin who made some changes, and presented it to Congress after the July 2 adoption of the independence section. The congressional revision process took all of July 3 and most of July 4, and the Declaration was adopted in the afternoon of July 4. [1]

## Printing, engrossing, and signing

The approved Declaration was printed on July 5 under the supervision of the Jefferson committee, and the printed copies, bearing only the names of President John Hancock and secretary Charles Thomson, were distributed to state assemblies, conventions, committees of safety, and commanding officers of the Continental troops. [1]

On July 19, Congress ordered the Declaration engrossed on parchment under the new title "the unanimous declaration of the thirteen united states of America" and directed that it be signed by every member of Congress. Engrossing is the process of copying an official document in a large hand; the engrosser was probably Timothy Matlock, an assistant to Thomson. [1]

On August 2, President Hancock signed the engrossed copy with a bold signature, and the other delegates, following custom, signed beginning at the right with signatures arranged by state from northernmost New Hampshire to southernmost Georgia. Not all delegates were present that day; 56 delegates eventually signed, and Elbridge Gerry, Oliver Wolcott, Lewis Morris, Thomas McKean, and Matthew Thornton signed late. Some delegates, including drafting committee member Livingston, never signed. [1]

## Structure and claims of the Declaration

The Declaration begins by holding these truths to be self-evident: that all men are created equal and are endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights, among them life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. [2]

It then argues that governments are instituted among men to secure these rights, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that whenever a government becomes destructive of these ends the people have the right to alter or abolish it and institute a new one. [2]

The middle of the document frames the history of the present King of Great Britain as a history of repeated injuries and usurpations aimed at establishing an absolute tyranny, and submits facts to a candid world. The grievances include refusing assent to laws necessary for the public good, dissolving representative houses repeatedly, keeping standing armies without consent, imposing taxes without consent, and depriving the people of trial by jury. [2]

In its conclusion the Declaration proclaims that the united colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states, absolved from all allegiance to the British Crown, with full power to levy war, conclude peace, contract alliances, and establish commerce. In support of the Declaration, the signers mutually pledged to each other their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor. [2]

## Display and later influence

The transcription published by the National Archives is based on the Stone Engraving of the parchment Declaration, and the document itself is on permanent display in the Rotunda of the National Archives Museum. [2]

Its principles continued to be invoked. In 1863, Abraham Lincoln explicitly invoked the Declaration of Independence and its principles of liberty and equality in the [Gettysburg Address](/hubpedia/gettysburg-address). [3]

- [Democratic rights](/hubpedia/democratic-rights)

articles.description: アメリカ合衆国憲法は、1787年夏にフィラデルフィアの憲法制定会議で秘密裏に起草され、同年9月17日に署名された四ページの文書で、アメリカ合衆国の政府を確立した。序文と七つの条文からなり、立法・行政・司法の三権分立と抑制均衡の仕組みを定め、九つの州の批准をもって発効した。世界で最も長命で最も模倣された憲法の一つとされる。

articles.summary: アメリカ合衆国憲法は、1787年夏にフィラデルフィアの憲法制定会議で秘密裏に起草され、同年9月17日に署名された四ページの文書で、アメリカ合衆国の政府を確立した。序文と七つの条文からなり、立法・行政・司法の三権分立と抑制均衡の仕組みを定め、九つの州の批准をもって発効した。世界で最も長命で最も模倣された憲法の一つとされる。
articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 概要

アメリカ合衆国憲法は、1787年夏に憲法制定会議の代表によって秘密裏に起草され、同年9月17日に署名された四ページの文書で、アメリカ合衆国の政府を確立した。文書の全四ページは国家公文書館に常設展示されている。 [1][4]

憲法は序文と、政府の構造と運用を定める七つの条文からなる。前三条が立法（議会）、行政（大統領府）、司法（連邦裁判所）の三権を確立し、権力の抑制と均衡の仕組みがいずれか一つの権力の支配を防ぐ。 [2]

## 歴史的背景

アメリカ最初の憲法である邦聯条例は、連合議会に規則制定と各州への資金要請の権能を与えていたが、執行権を持たず、通商を規制することも貨幣を発行することもできなかった。アレクサンダー・ハミルトンは、邦聯条例を修正するため各州代表の大会議を組織するよう議会を説得するのに助力した。 [3]

連邦会議は1787年5月14日、フィラデルフィアの州庁舎（独立記念館）で開会した。当初は二州の代表しか出席せず、5月25日に七州の定足数に達するまで日々延会を重ねた。 [1]

## 会議の経緯と妥協

代表たちは自由に発言できるよう州庁舎の窓を閉ざし、秘密を守ることを誓った。条例の修正のために集まったものの、議論を経て6月中旬までに、会議は全く新しい政府の枠組みを起草する方針を固めた。 [1][3]

主な争点は、中央政府にどれほどの権力を与えるか、議会における各州の議員数、そして議員を人民が直接選ぶか州議会が選ぶかという点だった。最も激しい論争は議会代表権をめぐるもので、妥協の結果、下院は人口三万人ごとに代表一名、上院は各州二名とされた。会議はまた、奴隷にされたアフリカ人を五分の三人として数えることに合意し、奴隷貿易は1808年まで継続可能とされた。 [1][3]

## 成文化と署名

三ヶ月の激論の後、代表は決定を文章化する細部委員会を任命し、会期末に近づくと風格・編成委員会が四日足らずの間に23条を七条に凝縮した。 [3]

1787年9月17日、38名の代表が憲法に署名した。ジョージ・リードが欠席したデラウェアのジョン・ディキンソンの分を署名したため、署名の総数は39となった。 [3]

## 七条の構造

序文は「われら合衆国の人民は、より完全な連合を形成し、正義を確立し」で始まり、憲法を制定する目的を列挙している。 [4]

第一条は立法権を議会に割り当てる。議会は下院と上院の二院からなり、この二院制は人口に基づく代表を望んだ大州と各州平等を望んだ小州との妥協だった。 [2]

第二条は行政部門と大統領・副大統領職を定め、選挙人団による大統領選出、被選資格（生来の市民で35歳以上）、任期の規則を定める。第三条は合衆国最高裁判所を頂点とする司法部門を設け、連邦裁判官を重罪がない限り終身とした。裁判所体系の詳細は第一議会に委ねられ、1789年の司法組織法が現在の三層裁判体系を作った。 [2]

第四条以降は州相互および州と連邦の関係を定め、第五条は法律制定より困難な修正手続を定める。修正案は連邦議会両院の各三分の二による提案、または三分の二の州議会の申請による全国会議で発せられ、四分の三の州議会または州会議の承認で批准される。第六条は連邦法が州・地方法に優越すると定め、第七条は批准手続を定めた。 [2]

## 批准への道

憲法制定者は国家政府への権限移譲を渋る州議会を迂回させ、各州の特別[批准](/hubpedia/ratification)会議に可否を委ねた。発効には13州中9州の批准が必要だったが、当時憲法支持多数を報告していたのは6州だけだった。 [3]

強い中央政府を必要と見る連邦派は少なくとも三州を転向させる必要があった。反連邦派は、打倒したばかりのものを思わせる強大な中央政府と[権利章典](/hubpedia/bill-of-rights)の欠如を理由に憲法に激しく反対した。形勢を変えたのはマサチューセッツ州で、「今批准し、後で修正する」という妥協が同州と最後の抵抗州での勝利をもたらした。ロードアイランドは1790年に13番目の批准州となった。 [2][3]

このようにして成立した憲法は、今日、世界で最も長命で最も模倣された憲法の一つとして立っている。 [3]

en.title: Constitution of the United States
en.summary: The Constitution of the United States is the four-page document drafted in secret by delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia during the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, 1787, establishing the government of the United States. It consists of a preamble and seven articles creating the legislative, executive, and judicial branches under a system of checks and balances, and it took effect upon ratification by nine states. It stands as one of the longest-lived and most emulated constitutions in the world.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Overview

The Constitution of the United States is the four-page document drafted in secret by delegates to the Constitutional Convention during the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, 1787, establishing the government of the United States. All four pages are on permanent display at the National Archives. [1][4]

The Constitution contains a preamble and seven articles describing how the government is structured and operates. The first three articles establish the legislative (Congress), executive (the presidency), and judicial (the federal courts) branches, and a system of checks and balances prevents any one of these powers from becoming dominant. [2]

## Historical background

America's first constitution, the Articles of Confederation, gave the Confederation Congress the power to make rules and request funds from the states, but it had no enforcement powers, could not regulate commerce, and could not print money. Alexander Hamilton helped convince Congress to organize a Grand Convention of state delegates to work on revising the Articles. [3]

The Federal Convention convened in the State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia on May 14, 1787. Because delegations from only two states were at first present, the members adjourned from day to day until a quorum of seven states was obtained on May 25. [1]

## Convention debates and compromises

The delegates shuttered the windows of the State House and swore secrecy so they could speak freely. Although they had gathered to revise the Articles, by mid-June they had decided to design an entirely new frame of government. [1][3]

The chief points at issue were how much power to allow the central government, how many representatives in Congress each state should have, and whether representatives would be elected directly by the people or by the state legislators. The fiercest argument was over congressional representation; the framers compromised by giving each state one representative for every 30,000 people in the House of Representatives and two in the Senate. They also agreed to count enslaved Africans as three-fifths of a person and allowed the slave trade to continue until 1808. [1][3]

## Drafting and signing

After three months of heated debate, the delegates appointed a Committee of Detail to put the decisions in writing, and near the end a Committee of Style and Arrangement condensed 23 articles into seven in less than four days. [3]

On September 17, 1787, 38 delegates signed the Constitution; George Reed signed for the absent John Dickinson of Delaware, bringing the total number of signatures to 39. [3]

## The seven articles

The Preamble begins "We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union, establish Justice" and enumerates the purposes for which the Constitution is ordained and established. [4]

Article I assigns lawmaking to Congress, divided into two houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate—a compromise between large states wanting representation by population and small ones wanting equal representation. [2]

Article II details the executive branch and the offices of President and Vice President, laying down rules for election through the Electoral College, eligibility (a natural-born citizen at least 35 years old), and term length. Article III establishes the judicial branch with the U.S. Supreme Court, specifies that federal judges serve for life unless they commit a serious crime, and left much of the court system's planning to the First Congress; the 1789 Judiciary Act created today's three-tiered system. [2]

The remaining articles cover the states' relations to each other and to the federal government. Article V explains the amendment process, which is harder than making laws: two-thirds of the Senate and House may propose an amendment, or two-thirds of the state legislatures may apply for a national convention, and three-fourths of the states must approve to ratify. Article VI makes federal law supreme over state and local laws, and Article VII describes the ratification process. [2]

## The road to ratification

The founders bypassed the state legislatures, reasoning their members would resist giving up power, and called for special [ratifying](/hubpedia/ratification) conventions in each state. Ratification by 9 of the 13 states would enact the new government, but at the time only 6 of 13 states reported a pro-Constitution majority. [3]

The Federalists, who believed a strong central government was necessary, needed to convert at least three states. The Anti-Federalists fought hard because the Constitution created a powerful central government reminiscent of the one they had just overthrown and lacked a [bill of rights](/hubpedia/bill-of-rights). The tide turned in Massachusetts, where the "vote now, amend later" compromise secured victory there and eventually in the final holdouts. Rhode Island became the 13th state to ratify in 1790. [2][3]

The Constitution thus created stands today as one of the longest-lived and most emulated constitutions in the world. [3]

articles.bodyMarkdown:
## 概要

ゲティスバーグ演説は、1863年11月19日、ペンシルベニア州ゲティスバーグの国立墓地の奉献式典で、エイブラハム・リンカーン大統領によって行われた演説である。式典は北軍の戦死者のための墓地を奉献するもので、ゲティスバーグは南北戦争で最も流血の多い戦いの一つの舞台だった。この記念の演説は、倒れた人々の新たに掘られた墓の上で行われた。 [1][2][3]

式典の主講演者は当時一流の雄弁家とされたエドワード・エヴァレットであり、彼は二時間以上話したのに対し、リンカーンは二分間話した。 [1]

## 奉献式典への招き

リンカーンは「国家の最高行政責任者として、若干の適切な言葉をもってこれらの土地をその神聖な用途のために正式に区切る」ために招かれた。 [1]

## 演説の主題と戦争の再定義

演説の中でリンカーンは[アメリカ独立宣言](/hubpedia/declaration-of-independence)とその自由と平等の原理を引用し、国にとっての「新しい自由の誕生」について語った。彼はアメリカ国民にとっての戦争の目的を再形成し続け、連合のための戦争から、連合と自由のための戦争へと変えていった。 [1]

## 文書の写本と記録

式典に関連して公開された文書は、リンカーンの私設秘書ジョン・ニコレイが所有していたもので、大統領の朗読用コピーと見なされている。この文書は1999年以来公開されておらず、連邦議会図書館からの特別貸出として展示された。 [1]

演説の第一草稿と見なされる二ページの写本（ニコレイ・コピー）は連邦議会図書館写本部が保管しており、インクで書き始められ鉛筆で終えられている。リンカーンの自筆による写しは少なくともさらに四部残存し、ヘイ・コピー（連邦議会図書館）、ブリス・コピー（ホワイトハウスのリンカーン寝室）、バンクロフト・コピー（コーネル大学図書館）、エヴァレット・コピー（イリノイ州スプリングフィールドのイリノイ州立歴史図書館）に所在する。これらの写しは「エイブラハム・リンカーン文書」の一部をなし、同文集は連邦議会図書館で97ロールのマイクロフィルムに収められている。 [2]

演説の高揚した言語は、もう一つのリンカーンの文書である[奴隷解放宣言](/hubpedia/emancipation-proclamation)の意図的に法律家的な文言と鋭い対照をなすとされる。 [2]

## 後世の評価と記念

リンカーン自身は当初この演説に不満を示したが、それは今日、合衆国史上最も優雅で雄弁な演説の一つと見なされるようになった。公文書館のプロログ誌の記事は、この文書を「内戦の単独で最も記憶に残る文書」と呼んでいる。 [1][2]

「アメリカを形づくった100の文書」の中から10のマイルストーン文書を選ぶ国民投票企画「The People's Vote」では、この文書がアメリカ史上8番目に重要な文書に選ばれた。同企画は2003年9月17日、憲法記念日に合衆国公文書館長ジョン・W・カーリンが発足させたものである。 [1]

演説の150周年にあたる2013年、フランクリン・D・ルーズベルト大統領図書館の記事はこれを「合衆国大統領による最大の演説の一つ」と位置づけた。ルーズベルトはその言葉を時代を超えたものと見出し、自らの時代の決定的な戦いを率いる中で、その約束から力と洞察を得たとされる。1938年7月3日、ゲティスバーグの戦い75周年にルーズベルトは「不滅の行為と不滅の言葉がここゲティスバーグにアメリカ愛国心の聖地を造った」と述べ、演説の一節「最後の全力を捧げた献身」に言及した。ルーズベルトはさらに、リンカーンがゲティスバーグで再確認した課題は、「人民の善のための人民の政府」という建国の目的を守る限り、この国家にとっての課題であり続けると語った。 [3]

2009年、公文書館75周年を記念する「BIG!」展はゲティスバーグ演説のセクションを設け、ゲティスバーグ戦場の巨大な地図と、墓地奉献式におけるリンカーンの貴重な写真を展示した。 [4]

en.title: Gettysburg Address
en.summary: The Gettysburg Address is the speech delivered by President Abraham Lincoln on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of the National Cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. While the featured speaker Edward Everett spoke for more than two hours, Lincoln spoke for two minutes. By invoking the Declaration of Independence's principles of liberty and equality and speaking of a "new birth of freedom," the address reshaped the war's aims and has come to be regarded as one of the most elegant and eloquent speeches in U.S. history.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Overview

The Gettysburg Address was delivered by President Abraham Lincoln on November 19, 1863, at a ceremony dedicating the National Cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The ceremony dedicated a cemetery for the Union war dead at the site of one of the bloodiest battles of the Civil War, and the commemorative speech was delivered over the freshly dug graves of the fallen. [1][2][3]

The featured speaker was Edward Everett, one of the nation's foremost orators; he spoke for more than two hours, while Lincoln spoke for two minutes. [1]

## The invitation to dedicate

Lincoln was invited "as Chief Executive of the nation, formally [to] set apart these grounds to their sacred use by a few appropriate remarks." [1]

## Themes and the redefinition of the war

In his address Lincoln invoked the [Declaration of Independence](/hubpedia/declaration-of-independence) and its principles of liberty and equality, and spoke of "a new birth of freedom" for the nation. He continued to reshape the aims of the war for the American people, transforming it from a war for Union to a war for Union and freedom. [1]

## Manuscripts and record copies

The document displayed in connection with the ceremony had belonged to John Nicolay, Lincoln's private secretary, and is believed to have been the President's reading copy. It had not been seen by the public since 1999 and was shown on special loan from the Library of Congress. [1]

The two pages of what is evidently the first draft, also called the Nicolay Copy, are held by the Manuscript Division of the Library of Congress and were started in ink and finished in pencil. At least four additional copies in Lincoln's hand survive: the Hay Copy at the Library of Congress, the Bliss Copy in the Lincoln bedroom of the White House, the Bancroft Copy at Cornell University Library, and the Everett Copy at the Illinois State Historical Library in Springfield. These copies form part of the Papers of Abraham Lincoln, which fill 97 rolls of microfilm at the Library of Congress. [2]

The soaring language of the address stands in sharp contrast to the deliberately legalistic wording of another towering Lincoln document, the [Emancipation Proclamation](/hubpedia/emancipation-proclamation). [2]

## Later assessment and commemoration

Although Lincoln initially expressed disappointment in the speech, it has come to be regarded as one of the most elegant and eloquent speeches in U.S. history. A National Archives Prologue article calls it the single most memorable document of the Civil War. [1][2]

In The People's Vote, a nationwide initiative inviting Americans to choose 10 milestone documents from a list of 100 documents that shaped America, the Gettysburg Address was voted the 8th most important document in American history. The program was launched by Archivist of the United States John W. Carlin on September 17, 2003, Constitution Day. [1]

On the 150th anniversary in 2013, a Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library article counted the address among the greatest speeches ever made by a US President, noting that FDR found Lincoln's words timeless and drew strength and insight from their promise while leading the country through the defining battles of his own time. On July 3, 1938, the 75th anniversary of the Battle of Gettysburg, Roosevelt declared that "immortal deeds and immortal words have created here at Gettysburg a shrine of American patriotism" and invoked the address's phrase "the last full measure of devotion." He added that the issue Lincoln restated at Gettysburg would remain before the nation so long as it clings to its founding purpose: "a people's government for the people's good." [3]

In 2009, the National Archives' 75th-anniversary exhibition BIG! included a section on the Gettysburg Address featuring an enormous map of the Gettysburg battlefield and a rare photograph of Lincoln at the dedication of the cemetery. [4]
